forms.artefact: The thing you produced, and what changed because of it.

skills.name: Roadmapping
skills.what: Turning strategy into a sequenced, time-boxed plan of what the team will build, and keeping it honest as reality changes.

subskills.name: Outcome-based roadmaps
subskills.example: Frame each quarter as problems to solve, not a list of features.

subskills.name: Sequencing & dependencies
subskills.example: Land the data pipeline before the dashboard that needs it.

subskills.name: Capacity & estimation
subskills.example: Size initiatives against real team throughput, with buffer for interrupts.

subskills.name: Roadmap communication
subskills.example: Publish a one-page roadmap plus a changelog of what moved and why.

subskills.name: Re-planning
subskills.example: Monthly check: what shipped, what slipped, what we learned, what changes.

ladder.associate: Owns a slice of the roadmap for one feature area; keeps the backlog and status current.
ladder.mid: Owns the quarterly roadmap for a product area; negotiates scope with engineering and design.
ladder.senior: Owns a multi-quarter roadmap tied to business goals; makes and defends cut decisions.
ladder.lead: Sets the roadmap across several teams; aligns it with company strategy and resourcing.

build: Course: a product fundamentals class that makes you produce a roadmap, not just read about one.
Project: write a Now/Next/Later roadmap for an app you use, with reasoning for the order.
At work: volunteer to run the planning doc for your team's next quarter.
signals: Owned the H2 roadmap for checkout; shipped 4 of 5 committed initiatives.
Re-sequenced the Q3 plan after a platform dependency slipped, protecting the launch date.

skills.name: Product strategy
skills.what: Choosing where to play and how to win: which customers, which problems, which bets, and what you will deliberately not do.

subskills.name: Writing a strategy
subskills.example: A 3-page memo: situation, bet, why now, what we'll stop doing.

subskills.name: Picking bets & trade-offs
subskills.example: Choose two bets for the year and name the three you're turning down.

subskills.name: Competitive positioning
subskills.example: Explain why your product wins against the top two alternatives.

subskills.name: Strategy to goals
subskills.example: Turn the strategy into 3 measurable objectives the team can own.

ladder.associate: Understands the team strategy well enough to explain why a feature matters.
ladder.mid: Contributes analysis and options to the area strategy; owns strategy for one feature line.
ladder.senior: Writes the strategy for a product area and gets leadership to fund it.
ladder.lead: Sets multi-year direction across products; decides what the org stops doing.

build: Read and rewrite: take a public strategy memo (e.g. a company's S-1 'why we win' section) and condense it to one page.
Project: write a strategy for a product you know, with explicit non-goals.
At work: draft the 'why now' section for your team's next big proposal.
signals: Authored the 2025 platform strategy adopted by three product teams.
Recommended sunsetting a legacy tier, redirecting 6 engineers to the growth bet.

measures: revenue or users the strategy reached

skills.name: Product vision
skills.what: Painting a credible picture of where the product is going in 2–5 years, vivid enough that teams can make decisions against it.

subskills.name: Vision narrative
subskills.example: A one-page 'press release from the future' the team can quote.

subskills.name: Aligning teams on the vision
subskills.example: Run the vision at kickoff and refer back to it in every trade-off.

subskills.name: Vision prototypes & demos
subskills.example: A clickable prototype of the product two years out.

ladder.associate: Can explain the product vision to a new engineer.
ladder.mid: Shapes the vision for a feature area within the product vision.
ladder.senior: Owns the product vision for an area and uses it to settle debates.
ladder.lead: Sets the vision for a product line and sells it to executives and customers.

build: Write a working-backwards press release for a product you'd build.
Study examples: Amazon PR/FAQ, Figma's early vision posts.
At work: propose the 2-year picture for your area at a planning offsite.
signals: Wrote the vision doc that reframed the team from 'reporting' to 'decision support'.
Produced the concept demo used in the Series B pitch.

skills.name: Prioritization & trade-offs
skills.what: Deciding what to do first, what to defer, and what to kill, with a rationale others can check, under constraints you don't control.

subskills.name: Prioritization frameworks
subskills.example: Score the backlog on reach, impact, confidence, effort, then sanity-check by hand.

subskills.name: Saying no with reasons
subskills.example: Decline an exec request in writing with the trade it would force.

subskills.name: Trade-off analysis
subskills.example: Lay out the two options, what each costs, and what you'd give up.

subskills.name: Backlog management
subskills.example: Keep the top 20 items ready, estimated, and in order.

ladder.associate: Keeps a prioritized backlog for one feature and can justify the top five.
ladder.mid: Decides what a squad works on each sprint and quarter.
ladder.senior: Makes cut decisions across competing stakeholders and absorbs the pushback.
ladder.lead: Allocates teams and budget across initiatives; decides what the org drops.

build: Project: take 30 feature requests for a known app, score them with RICE, write the top-5 rationale.
Practice: for any request, write the 'what we'd have to give up' sentence.
At work: run backlog refinement for a sprint and publish the order with reasons.
signals: Cut scope 40% to hit the compliance deadline; shipped the deferred items next quarter.
Introduced a weighted scoring model that ended the weekly 'what's next' debate.

software.reads_as: Choosing what to build, fix or pay down next: features against reliability work and technical debt.
software.line: Ranked 30 reliability and debt items against the roadmap; shipped the top 8 in a quarter and cut pages by 40%.

data_ai.reads_as: Choosing which model, dataset or eval to work on next, by what moves the product metric.
data_ai.line: Picked 3 of 12 model experiments by expected lift; the first raised offline recall 6 points and shipped in 5 weeks.

security.reads_as: Ranking risks and findings by exploitability and impact, so the team fixes what matters first.
security.line: Triaged 400 findings by exploitability into a top-20 list; closed all 20 critical issues within 30 days.

design.reads_as: Choosing which flows and problems get design time, and how much polish each deserves.
design.line: Cut a 14-screen redesign to the 4 flows behind 70% of support tickets; shipped them in one release.

legal.reads_as: Triaging legal requests by risk and business value with a small team and a long queue.
legal.line: Set up intake and a risk tier for 600 contract requests a year; cut median turnaround from 9 days to 3.

skills.name: PRDs & requirements writing
skills.what: Writing the document that tells engineering and design exactly what problem to solve, for whom, with what constraints, and how we'll know it worked.

subskills.name: Problem statements
subskills.example: One paragraph: who, what hurts, how often, what it costs them.

subskills.name: User stories & acceptance criteria
subskills.example: As a seller, I can refund an order within 30 days; refund posts within 24h.

subskills.name: Edge cases & non-functional requirements
subskills.example: What happens when the payment fails mid-flow, or the user is offline.

subskills.name: Success metrics in the spec
subskills.example: Ship when refund completion rate is above 95% in beta.

subskills.name: Spec reviews
subskills.example: Walk engineering through the doc before a line of code is written.

ladder.associate: Writes clear tickets and small specs for well-understood features.
ladder.mid: Writes full PRDs for a feature; runs the review with engineering and design.
ladder.senior: Writes specs for ambiguous, multi-team problems; sets the bar for the team's docs.
ladder.lead: Rarely writes PRDs; reviews them and defines what a good one looks like.

build: Course: a technical writing or product spec workshop (Google's technical writing course is free).
Project: write a PRD for a feature you wish an app had, including edge cases and metrics.
At work: offer to spec a small feature end to end and run the review.
signals: Wrote 12 PRDs in 2024; zero launched features required a post-launch requirements change.
Introduced a PRD template with acceptance criteria that cut QA back-and-forth by half.

measures: features shipped without a requirements change

skills.name: End-to-end product lifecycle
skills.what: Taking a product from idea through discovery, build, launch, growth, and eventually retirement, and knowing what each stage needs.

subskills.name: Zero-to-one
subskills.example: Validate a problem, ship a narrow MVP, find the first 10 paying users.

subskills.name: Scaling a product
subskills.example: Move from manual onboarding to self-serve without losing conversion.

subskills.name: Deprecation & sunsetting
subskills.example: Migrate users off the old API with a 6-month notice and tooling.

subskills.name: Post-launch iteration
subskills.example: Hold a 30-day review and ship the three biggest fixes.

ladder.associate: Has shipped features and seen one full cycle from spec to post-launch review.
ladder.mid: Has taken a feature from discovery through launch and iteration, end to end.
ladder.senior: Has taken a product or major surface from zero to scale, including hard retirements.
ladder.lead: Manages a portfolio at different lifecycle stages and staffs each appropriately.

build: Project: ship something real end to end (a side project, a no-code tool, an internal tool) and write up each stage.
Read: 'Inspired' (Cagan) for the stages; 'The Lean Startup' for 0-to-1.
At work: ask to own a small feature from discovery through launch metrics review.
signals: Took the referrals product from concept to 15% of new signups in 9 months.
Led the deprecation of v1 API across 400 integrators with zero escalations.

artefacts: a feature taken from discovery to launch

skills.name: Product launches
skills.what: Getting a product out the door: readiness, staged rollout, enablement, announcement, and the follow-through once real users hit it.

subskills.name: Launch planning & readiness
subskills.example: A checklist covering support docs, legal review, analytics, and rollback.

subskills.name: Staged rollouts & feature flags
subskills.example: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with go/no-go metrics at each step.

subskills.name: Launch communications
subskills.example: Release notes written for users, not for engineers.

subskills.name: Launch monitoring
subskills.example: A dashboard watched for 48 hours with an agreed rollback trigger.

ladder.associate: Runs launch checklists and writes release notes for small features.
ladder.mid: Owns the launch of a feature end to end, including rollout and monitoring.
ladder.senior: Runs multi-team launches with external announcements and executive visibility.
ladder.lead: Sets launch standards and tiers for the org; owns flagship launches.

build: Project: write a launch plan for a feature in an app you use, with rollout stages and a rollback rule.
Study: public launch retros and 'what went wrong' write-ups.
At work: own the checklist and comms for your team's next release.
signals: Launched the new onboarding to 100% in 3 weeks with no P1 incidents via a staged rollout.
Ran 14 feature launches in 2024 with release notes and support enablement for each.

skills.name: Feature definition & scoping
skills.what: Deciding what's in and out of a feature so it solves the problem without ballooning: the minimum that proves the idea.

subskills.name: MVP scoping
subskills.example: Ship the single most common path first; defer the settings page.

subskills.name: Scope control
subskills.example: When the estimate doubles, cut features rather than slip the date.

subskills.name: User flows & states
subskills.example: Map the happy path, the error path, and the empty state before design starts.

ladder.associate: Scopes small features with guidance; writes clear tickets.
ladder.mid: Defines an MVP and defends the cut list with engineering and design.
ladder.senior: Scopes complex, multi-team features and finds the thin slice others missed.
ladder.lead: Reviews scoping decisions across teams; coaches PMs to cut harder.

build: Exercise: take any feature idea and write three versions: 1-week, 1-month, 1-quarter.
Project: build a tiny version of something with no-code tools and note what you cut.
At work: propose the smaller first release of whatever is being planned.
signals: Cut the initial release to 3 of 9 requested capabilities; shipped 6 weeks early and validated demand.
Defined the MVP for the mobile app that reached 10k users before the full build.

skills.name: Customer obsession / user empathy
skills.what: Making decisions from the customer's point of view, backed by direct contact with them, rather than from internal convenience.

subskills.name: Regular customer contact
subskills.example: Two customer conversations a week, every week, logged and shared.

subskills.name: Voice of the customer
subskills.example: A weekly digest of top complaints from support, sales, and app reviews.

subskills.name: Advocating internally
subskills.example: Bring a real customer recording into the planning meeting.

ladder.associate: Reads support tickets and joins customer calls; can describe the top three pain points.
ladder.mid: Runs a steady customer contact habit and brings it into every spec.
ladder.senior: Builds the team's customer feedback loop and uses it to change priorities.
ladder.lead: Keeps the org close to customers at scale: advisory boards, exec visits, feedback programs.

build: Habit: interview 5 people who use any product you care about; write up what surprised you.
Volunteer: do a support shift or read 50 app-store reviews and cluster them.
At work: sit in on sales or support calls weekly and share a digest.
signals: Ran 80 customer interviews in a year; three roadmap items came directly from them.
Started a weekly 'voice of customer' digest read by 60 people across the company.

skills.name: Product sense & judgment
skills.what: Judgment about what makes a product good: spotting the right problem, the elegant solution, and the detail that will annoy users.

subskills.name: Product critique
subskills.example: Tear down a competitor's onboarding and explain each choice they made.

subskills.name: Simplicity & craft
subskills.example: Remove a step from a flow rather than add a tooltip explaining it.

subskills.name: Spotting opportunities
subskills.example: Notice that 30% of users export to a spreadsheet and build the thing they do there.

ladder.associate: Can explain why a product decision is good or bad with specifics.
ladder.mid: Makes solid product calls on features; rarely needs the decision reversed.
ladder.senior: Trusted for judgment on ambiguous calls; raises the quality bar of the team.
ladder.lead: Sets the product quality bar for the org; final say on taste decisions.

Mock interviews: 'improve X' and 'design Y for Z' product-sense questions.
At work: review designs early and give specific, reasoned feedback.
signals: Redesigned the checkout flow from 6 steps to 3; conversion up 18%.
Published weekly product teardowns followed by 2k readers.

skills.name: UX & design collaboration
skills.what: Working with designers as a partner: framing the problem, reviewing work with specifics, and understanding enough of the craft to be useful.

subskills.name: Design briefs
subskills.example: Hand design a problem and constraints, not a sketch of the solution.

subskills.name: Prototyping & wireframes
subskills.example: Build a clickable Figma prototype to test before engineering starts.

subskills.name: Usability testing
subskills.example: Watch five users attempt the task and count where they get stuck.

subskills.name: Design systems & accessibility
subskills.example: Know when a new pattern is justified versus reusing the system.

ladder.associate: Reviews designs and gives specific feedback; can make a wireframe.
ladder.mid: Runs design kickoffs and usability tests with a design partner.
ladder.senior: Shapes the design strategy for an area; prototypes to test big ideas.
ladder.lead: Partners with design leadership on quality bar and resourcing.

build: Course: an intro UX course that includes running a usability test.
Tool: learn Figma well enough to wireframe and prototype a flow.
At work: run a 5-user usability test on an existing feature and share findings.
signals: Ran 12 usability sessions that reshaped the onboarding flow before build.
Prototyped the new dashboard in Figma and validated it with 8 customers.

skills.name: Structured problem solving
skills.what: Breaking an ambiguous situation into parts, finding the real cause, and choosing an approach when the answer isn't obvious.

subskills.name: Root-cause analysis
subskills.example: Trace a conversion drop to a slow API, not the new button colour.

subskills.name: Structuring problems
subskills.example: Lay out the three possible causes and what evidence would settle each.

subskills.name: Working through ambiguity
subskills.example: Turn 'make it better' into a concrete problem statement in a week.

subskills.name: Decision making
subskills.example: Decide reversible things fast; slow down only for the irreversible ones.

ladder.associate: Breaks down well-defined problems; asks good questions on fuzzy ones.
ladder.mid: Structures ambiguous feature problems and proposes a path with evidence.
ladder.senior: Solves cross-team, poorly defined problems; known for clear thinking.
ladder.lead: Frames org-level problems and sets the decision process for others.

Exercise: write up a problem you solved as situation → analysis → decision → result.

signals: Diagnosed a 12% activation drop to an email deliverability change within two days.
Turned a vague 'fix retention' mandate into three testable hypotheses and a plan.

subskills.example: Build a working prototype of the feature in an afternoon to test with users.

subskills.example: Synthesize 40 interview transcripts with an LLM, then verify by hand.

subskills.name: AI-native workflows
subskills.example: Automate the weekly update draft from the ticket tracker.

build: Build something with Cursor, Claude Code, or Replit this week; the only way to learn is to use them.
Project: prototype a feature idea with AI tools and test it with 5 users.
At work: pick one recurring task and automate it with an LLM.
signals: Prototyped 6 feature concepts with AI tools in Q1; 2 shipped after user tests.
Built an LLM pipeline that tags and summarizes support tickets daily.

skills.name: 2+ years experience
skills.what: Entry-level: internships, rotational programs, and first PM roles ask for up to two years of related experience.
build: Internships, APM programs, and adjacent roles (analyst, support, engineering) all count.
A shipped side project with users is the strongest substitute.
signals: 2 years as a data analyst supporting the product team.

skills.name: 3+ years experience
skills.what: Early-career: three to four years, usually with at least one full product cycle owned.
build: Own one feature end to end and be able to tell its story with numbers.
signals: 3 years of product management across two B2B products.

skills.name: 5+ years experience
skills.what: Mid-career: five to six years, the standard ask for a Senior PM.
build: Multiple launches, measurable impact, and cross-team leadership examples.
signals: 5+ years in product management, including 2 years leading a platform area.

skills.name: 8+ years experience
skills.what: Experienced: seven to nine years, typical for staff, principal, group, and many director roles.
build: Evidence of strategy ownership and of growing others.
signals: 8 years of product experience, last 3 as Group PM over 3 squads.

skills.name: 10+ years experience
skills.what: Senior leadership: ten or more years, usually director and above.
build: Org-level results, hiring and leveling, and P&L or budget ownership.
signals: 12 years in product, including 5 leading teams of 10+ PMs.

skills.name: Prior product management experience
skills.what: Prior product-management experience specifically, as opposed to adjacent roles.
build: If you don't have the title yet: APM programs, internal transfers, or a hybrid role (TPM, analyst, founder) where you owned product decisions.
Document the product decisions you made in your current role; that's PM experience in all but name.
signals: 4 years as a Product Manager at two companies; owned roadmap, specs, and launches.

skills.name: Bachelor's degree
skills.what: A bachelor's degree, often 'or equivalent practical experience'.
build: Most postings accept equivalent experience; make the equivalence explicit on your resume.
signals: B.A. Economics, University of X.

skills.name: Master's / MBA
skills.what: An MBA or master's, preferred more often than required, and more common in strategy-heavy and enterprise roles.
build: Worth it mainly for a career pivot or a specific network; part-time and online options are increasingly accepted.
signals: MBA, with a concentration in technology strategy.

skills.name: PhD / research background
skills.what: A PhD or research background, asked for in AI research-adjacent product roles.
build: Relevant mainly for research-lab product roles; a strong publication record or research engineering experience is the practical substitute.
signals: PhD in Computer Science (NLP); 3 publications.

skills.name: CS / engineering degree or background
skills.what: A computer science or engineering degree, or an engineering background, asked for by technical PM and TPM roles.
build: Without the degree: a software engineering stint, a bootcamp plus shipped code, or a technical certification plus evidence you read and discuss code.
signals: B.S. Computer Science; 2 years as a backend engineer before moving to product.

skills.name: Startup / scale-up experience
skills.what: Having worked at an early-stage or high-growth company, as evidence you can operate with little structure.
build: Join one, found one, or do a meaningful project with one; hackathons and accelerators count at the margin.
signals: Employee #8 at a seed-stage fintech; built the product function through Series A.

skills.name: Large-scale / big-tech experience
skills.what: Experience at scale: products with millions of users or large organizations.
build: A role at a large platform, or ownership of a high-traffic surface anywhere.
signals: PM at a top-5 tech company on a surface with 50M MAU.

skills.name: Consulting / banking / finance background
skills.what: A consulting, banking, or strategy background, valued for structured thinking and executive communication.
build: Not required; the transferable parts are structured problem solving and business cases, both of which you can show directly.
signals: 2 years at a strategy consultancy before product.

skills.name: Security clearance / citizenship
skills.what: A security clearance or U.S. person status, required for defense and some government work.
build: Clearances are sponsored by employers; being clearable (citizenship, clean record) is what you can control.
signals: Active Secret clearance.

skills.name: Deep domain expertise required
skills.what: Deep knowledge of the industry the product serves, often weighted above generic PM skills in regulated or specialized markets.
build: Pick a domain and go deep: work in it, read its regulation and economics, talk to its practitioners.
Adjacent roles in the domain (ops, analyst, clinician, trader) are often the best path into domain PM.
signals: 6 years in healthcare operations before moving into health-tech product.
